newsitem.title: FRANCE: YACHTING-LEADER NEARS PORT IN VENDEE GLOBE SAILING RACE.
newsitem.headline: YACHTING-LEADER NEARS PORT IN VENDEE GLOBE SAILING RACE.

text.p: The leader in the solo round-the-world Vendee Globe sailing race, marked by dramatic rescues and the disappearance of a competitor, said on Friday he would reach port in western France on Sunday.
Christophe Auguin, the skipper of Geodis, is set to complete the race in 105 days, breaking the 109-day race record set in 1989 by another French sailor, Titouan Lamazou.
"I have hit the winter. Winds are 45 knots and waves are size XL," Auguin radioed from his yacht as he sailed at 14 knots off western Spain.
He said he was sleeping barely three hours a day, wary of a collision after his radar broke down near Cape Horn.
The other competitors were hundreds of miles behind him.
The accident-prone third Vendee Globe Challenge, through lonely, towering seas fraught with dangerous icebergs, has confirmed its reputation as one of the world's most dangerous sports events.

Only seven of the 16 competitors are still in the race which skirts southern Africa, rounds Antarctica clockwise towards Cape Horn to end in Les Sables d'Olonne, on France's Atlantic coast, where it started on November 3.
Canadian Gerry Roufs has been missing for 36 days. He was last in contact with organisers when in a remote Antarctic area between New Zealand and Cape Horn in some of the world's heaviest seas.
Reports that a Chilean air force plane had made radio contact with a boat that could be Roufs' near the southern tip of South America last month were later denied.
Two other competitors, Frenchman Thierry Dubois and Briton Tony Bullimore, were plucked from the sea by the Australian navy in dramatic rescues after their boats capsized southwest of Australia.
Another Frenchman, Raphael Dinelli, was rescued by fellow competitor Pete Goss and taken to Tasmania.
Most other competitors had to make for land after breaking equipment in collisions with unidentified objects or animals. Some of them, although disqualified, have resumed the race.
The accidents, and the costly and risky rescues, have triggered charges that the French-organised race was too dangerous and that yacht builders had sacrificed safety to speed.
Some critics have suggested the race's route should be modified to ban competitors from sailing so far south. Others have said it should be abandoned altogether.

French Sports Minister Guy Drut has opposed scrapping the race, saying sailors were aware of the risks they took. But he said organisers and shipbuilders would have to take a deep look at the conditions of the next race to improve safety.

The French Yachting Federation said it would organise a meeting of world yachting associations, Australian rescuers, weather experts, foreign race organisers, competitors and navy officials in the spring to review safety problems.
